name: Photo lighting / golden hour
lead: Photo lighting is the choice of light used when a face is photographed, and golden hour is the best-known version: the period shortly after sunrise or before sunset when daylight is redder and softer than at midday [1]. People use it to look better in photos, because low-contrast, warm light leaves shadows less dark and highlights less likely to blow out, which makes skin and facial features read more evenly [1].

Portrait photographers have long managed light for this purpose. Nineteenth-century sitters were lit by soft overhead window light, a window and a reflector are described as enough for amateurs and professionals, and a white reflector bounces light into the darker side of the face to even out contrast [2]. Midday sun produces strong highlights and dark shadows that portrait photographers often offset with fill flash [1].

In looksmaxxing and photo-presentation circles, soft window, shade or evening light is a common way to improve dating-profile and social photos without changing the face. No studies were found that test lighting choice against perceived attractiveness.
infobox: Shortly after sunrise or before sunset [1]
About 3,500 K at golden hour versus about 5,500 K at midday [1]

paras: When the sun is low its rays cross more atmosphere, which weakens direct light. More of the illumination then comes from indirect skylight, lowering the lighting ratio, and more blue light is scattered so the sun looks reddish [1]. Contrast is lower, so shadows are less dark and highlights less likely to be overexposed, and the low angle produces longer shadows [1].

The 'hour' is figurative. Its length varies with season and latitude, and planning tools define it by sun altitude, for example 0 to 6 or 0 to 10 degrees above the horizon [1]. Cinematographer Nestor Almendros described the related 'magic hour' on Days of Heaven as lasting about twenty minutes a day [1]. The blue hour just before sunrise or after sunset has mostly blue light and no sharp shadows [1].

Window light has been used for portraits for decades; early morning and late afternoon are described as the best times, and curtains, reflectors and shields soften it [2]. In studio setups the key light sits roughly 30 to 60 degrees from the camera, a fill light or reflector opposite it reduces shadows, and softboxes give softer light than open strobes [2].

Butterfly lighting, with the key above the camera and fill below, was a favourite of Hollywood portraitist George Hurrell and is also called Paramount lighting [2]. High-key lighting gives a mostly shadow-free image, while low-key lighting produces dark shadows [2].

Appearance communities discuss photo lighting alongside angles, lenses and editing as part of presenting the face well in profile pictures. Proponents say soft directional light reduces harsh shadows under the eyes and along the jaw, and that midday overhead sun does the opposite. These are practitioner views; the sources cited here describe the lighting effects in general terms rather than for faces specifically.

lore.intro: Soft or golden light is a recurring suggestion in photo-presentation advice.

claims.claim: Soft golden-hour light makes faces look better in photos
claims.believers: Proponents say low, warm light softens shadows and skin texture, so the face photographs more evenly.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports lower contrast, less dark shadows and fewer blown highlights at golden hour, and notes it is often preferred for portraits [1]. No published study has tested the effect on perceived attractiveness.

claims.believers: Photographers and users say strong overhead light creates harsh shadows.
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes midday sun creates strong highlights and dark shadows that portrait photographers often counter with fill flash [1].

card.summary: Shooting in soft, low-angle light to flatter your face on camera; physics is clear, the attractiveness payoff is untested.

quick.overview:
Golden hour is the soft, warm light near sunrise and sunset. Photographers favour it for portraits because it lowers contrast and softens shadows.

Whether it makes people look more attractive in photos has not been studied.
quick.mechanism: Low sun passes through more atmosphere, so light is warmer and more diffuse, with gentler shadows.[1]
quick.risks: No health risks. The only caveat is that effects on perceived attractiveness are unmeasured.

chain: Low sun or diffused window light lowers contrast
Shadows under the brow, eyes and jaw are softer
Face looks more even and flattering in the photo
angle.text: Choosing soft, low-angle or diffused light changes how a face is rendered in a photo: shadows are lighter and highlights less harsh [1][2]. People apply it to profile and social photos to present their features at their best.
